events.title: The Florida recount
events.text: Florida's presidential count ended with George W. Bush ahead by 537 votes out of almost six million.

events.title: Bush v. Gore
events.text: On 12 December the Supreme Court halted the Florida recount, settling the presidential election.

events.title: A rare midterm gain
events.text: The president's party gained House seats in a midterm, as it had in 1998: the only two such gains since 1946.

events.title: Help America Vote Act
events.text: Congress set national standards for voting equipment and created the Election Assistance Commission.

events.title: Ohio decides
events.text: Ohio's electoral votes, won by about two points, decided the presidential election.

events.title: Democrats take Congress
events.text: In the midterms Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate.

events.title: Indiana turns
events.text: Indiana voted Democratic for president for the first time since 1964.

events.title: Grant Park
events.text: Barack Obama, elected the first Black president, spoke to supporters in Chicago.

events.title: Citizens United
events.text: The Supreme Court ruled that independent political spending by corporations and unions cannot be banned.

events.title: A 63-seat wave
events.text: Republicans gained sixty-three House seats and the majority, the most in a midterm since 1938.

events.title: Obama re-elected
events.text: Barack Obama won a second term, carrying 26 states and Washington, D.C.

events.title: Shelby County v. Holder
events.text: The Supreme Court ended federal pre-clearance of election changes in states with a history of discrimination.

events.title: Republicans win the Senate
events.text: Republicans gained nine Senate seats and took control of the chamber.

events.title: Pennsylvania turns
events.text: Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin voted Republican for president for the first time since the 1980s.

events.title: Trump elected
events.text: Donald Trump won the Electoral College while Hillary Clinton won the national popular vote.

events.title: Alabama special election
events.text: A Democrat won a Senate seat in Alabama for the first time in twenty-five years.

events.title: The 2018 wave
events.text: Democrats gained forty-one House seats; turnout, about half of eligible voters, was the highest for a midterm since 1914.

events.title: Ranked-choice debut
events.text: Maine became the first state to use ranked-choice voting in a general election for Congress.

events.title: Arizona and Georgia flip
events.text: Joe Biden carried Arizona and Georgia, both by less than half a point.

events.title: Record mail voting
events.text: During the pandemic more Americans than ever before voted by mail.

events.title: Georgia runoffs
events.text: Two Senate runoffs won by Democrats on 5 January produced a 50–50 Senate.

events.title: The Capitol breached
events.text: On 6 January a crowd broke into the Capitol as Congress met to count the electoral votes.

events.title: New House apportionment
events.text: The 2020 census moved seven House seats: Texas gained two, five states one each, and seven states lost one.

events.title: Dobbs decision
events.text: The Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, returning abortion law to the states.

events.title: Kansas abortion vote
events.text: Kansas voters rejected a constitutional amendment on abortion by about eighteen points.

events.title: A narrow House majority
events.text: Republicans gained nine House seats and the majority; Democrats gained one Senate seat.

events.title: Speaker removed
events.text: For the first time, the House voted to remove its Speaker in the middle of a term.

events.title: Seven swing states
events.text: Donald Trump carried all seven of the closest states and won the national popular vote by 1.5 points.

events.title: Senate changes hands
events.text: Republicans gained four Senate seats, including Montana's, for a 53–47 majority.

events.title: Tax law signed
events.text: A tax and spending law passed the House 218–214 and the Senate 51–50; the CBO estimates it adds $3.4 trillion to deficits over ten years.

events.title: Texas redraws its map
events.text: Texas adopted new House districts in the middle of the decade; the Supreme Court allowed them for 2026.

events.title: Longest shutdown
events.text: The federal government was shut down for forty-three days, from 1 October to 12 November, the longest on record.

events.title: California's Proposition 50
events.text: California voters approved new, legislature-drawn House districts for 2026 to 2030.

events.title: Virginia elects a governor
events.text: A Democrat won Virginia's governorship, which had been held by a Republican.

events.title: Indiana says no
events.text: Indiana's state Senate rejected a new congressional map, thirty-one votes to nineteen.

events.title: Utah court map
events.text: A state court adopted new House districts for Utah after striking down the 2021 map.

events.title: Tariff ruling
events.text: On 20 February the Supreme Court ruled six to three that the emergency-powers law does not authorise tariffs.

events.title: Louisiana v. Callais
events.text: On 29 April the Supreme Court narrowed how the Voting Rights Act applies to House districts drawn by race.

events.title: Florida redraws
events.text: Florida adopted a new House map in May; its supreme court declined to block it for 2026.

events.title: Late mail ballots
events.text: In Watson v. RNC the Supreme Court let states count mail ballots postmarked by Election Day and received later.

events.title: Missouri's map paused
events.text: Missouri votes on 2022 district lines after a referendum petition on its new map; the map itself is on the ballot.

events.title: Election Day
events.text: On 3 November polls close from 6 p.m. Eastern in parts of Indiana and Kentucky to 1 a.m. in Alaska's Aleutians.

events.title: Possible Georgia runoff
events.text: In Georgia a candidate needs a majority; if no one has one, the top two meet again on 1 December.

chartNote: Each state is coloured by the margin of the most recent presidential popular vote (Democratic minus Republican share of all votes; FEC certified results, compiled by the MIT Election Data and Science Lab). It is a simplification: a midterm elects House members district by district, and senators and governors in their own races, so the presidential margin is a backdrop, not a forecast. Shares are of land area, not of people or votes: large rural states fill much of the map. Boundaries are today's (Census TIGER-based Natural Earth); Alaska and Hawaii are shown as insets.
